t: Why You Should Allow Your Students To Socialize In Class
q: However, when narrowly defined, giving your students the option to talk with their friends for a minute or two during the school day is a smart idea.
60-90 seconds or so is all it takes to “clear the boards.” It purges their thoughts from being dominated by what they desperately want to tell their friends.
Sitting too long causes excitability and restlessness. Short breaks throughout the day relax the body, clear the mind, and promote better listening and production.
It’s the Law of Reciprocity in action. Meaning, they’ll want to pay you back for your kindness and understanding.
You must teach and model exactly what one minute (or more) of socializing looks like.

t: Team Members Who Are Afraid of Disagreement
q: Although it is sometimes hard for leaders to fully grasp, some team members are simply afraid of disagreement.
Consider that some team members fear disagreement because they are afraid of being judged or rejected.
A belief that disagreement may weaken bonds and harm relationships can serve as a major impediment.
Playful arguing over favorite shows, service providers, music preferences, and current news events provides these team members with the necessary practice
Without disagreement, people and teams don’t make progress. Learning that can be a life-changer for those frightened by debate.

t: Leaders Who Confuse Being Kind With Being Agreeable
q: However, kindness also makes room for honesty, accountability, and challenge, all to the benefit of others.
People who confuse the two qualities often make a mess of leadership.
True concern for others frequently demands a blunt honesty, which can be at odds with the desire to be liked
as a rule, good leaders focus less on comfort and more on truth . This makes them less agreeable
Leaders who lack kindness are often hard to bear. Leaders who overly promote agreeableness are often hard to follow.

t: Deciding on the Time to Decide
q: Leaders who succumb to the pressure to “do something” — to act decisively — typically regret it later.
When leaders and groups are faced with so much uncertainty that they can’t act, the wise choice is to decide on the time to decide .
A decision schedule reduces ambiguity, mobilizes commitment, and puts people at ease.
Once team members throughout the organization know a timeline for decision-making has been set, they stop second-guessing the inaction
Deciding on the time to decide is one of the most important choices leaders and teams make when confronting a quicksand of uncertainty.

t: How to Determine Your Leader’s Risk Appetite
q: Knowing the risk appetite of a leader is central intelligence , as it helps team members decide what proposals and ideas to push forward
Leaders with a higher risk appetite tend to make bolder moves and allocate resources to innovative and unproven initiatives
Another observation to make is how often the leader speaks about problems versus opportunities
Those with a higher risk appetite generally move on quickly from disappointments and focus more on what to do next time
Risk is the price leaders pay for opportunity. Always remember that some are willing to pay more than others.

t: Taking a Moment for Reflection
q: This gives them the chance to collect their thoughts and convey the message they want to send, not the one that pops into their head.
The pause also interrupts emotional reactions of both parties and typically lowers the temperature of the discussion just enough to make a difference.
It takes maturity, emotional intelligence, and sound judgment to take such a pause, and everyone involved knows it.
Notice the statements are not a request. Leaders claim the right to pause as they see fit.
Leaders who too often allow themselves to get caught up in the emotion or enthusiasm of the moment without taking a moment for reflection often regret their responses and decisions

t: Dont Let AI Transcription Sink Your Ship
q: What was unheard of a few short years ago is now a reality for any virtual and live meetings.
Whatever gets said or discussed is now on permanent record, including the candid remarks a leader or team member makes during a heated exchange.
Legal risks rise because the transcripts place leaders on record for the reasons (good and bad) behind their decisions.
Because transcriptions and their summaries miss the critical human elements that give rise to meaning, such as tone, emotion, and sarcasm, they often distort what actually happened.
Many meetings and conversations are automatically recorded and transcribed without the awareness of the attendees.

t: Seeking Sweet and Sour Feedback
q: So, good leaders conduct a listening tour, where they meet with individuals and groups to hear what they have to say.
Resistance is magnified any time a leader makes changes before absorbing the views and opinions of the team members and stakeholders.
Sweet and sour feedback is a powerful metaphor for learning about what is going well and what needs improvement or attention.
Framing the question as seeking sweet and sour feedback is a great setup for asking a two-sided question: What is the best of the place, and what is the worst of the place?
Once they know the current state, leaders are primed to make changes. But not a minute before then.

t: Why You Should Never Allow Students To Make Up Work
q: But allowing students to retake tests, make up assignments, and ignore deadlines is something you should never do.
Your students can’t stay up to date with your current lessons when they haven’t mastered the previous and prerequisite material.
By giving chance after chance, you’re very effectively teaching students to be lazy, undisciplined, and unemployable. Discipline is learned through hard deadlines.
Without goals, objectives, and due dates with real stakes, life very quickly loses meaning.
Without standards to meet, students become entitled. They begin to believe that everything can be put off, ignored, or negotiated to their liking.
Although a gift your students may not understand or appreciate until years later, holding them to a standard required for success in school and beyond is nonetheless precious.

t: Thinking About Perpendicular Bisectors
q: I was never satisfied with simply teaching constructions as step-by-step processes for pupils to follow, reproduce, and memorise.
Even when pupils successfully reproduced and memorised my step-by-step process, I found they often struggled to adapt it when they faced with other, less familiar constructions.
It felt like the compasses were a distraction from learning how to construct perpendicular bisectors.

Rather than the sole objective of the lesson being to 'learn how to construct a perpendicular bisector using a pair of compasses and a ruler', the primary objective would be to 'explore what happens when circles intersect'.

One of these is that kites have a line of symmetry which (in the case of these constructions) passes through the centre of each circle. Additionally, the two diagonals of a kite are always perpendicular.
While I did usually summarise by outlining a step-by-step method towards the end of the lesson, most pupils didn’t seem to need it.

t: The Spacing Calculator
q: We see five-minute starters or Do Nows. Five minutes of recall; five minutes of learning. Then the lesson moves on, and the next topic begins.

As a very rough estimate, to help build permanent and resilient memory, we should be aiming for 5 or more opportunities for retrieval of any given topic, spaced close enough that pupils do not forget but the memory still builds.
It was perfect in theory but completely unsustainable in practice, the document was completely overwhelming to look at and basically impossible to understand efficiently.
Between 2 and 3 (can be a decimal), based on difficulty. Harder topics get tighter spacing (a multiplier closer to 2), easier ones get longer intervals (a multiplier closer to 3).
There is enough time in the curriculum to retrieve properly. It just requires reconsidering some entrenched assumptions.
We’ve pretended for too long that retrieval can be done on instinct. It can’t. It needs structure.

t: Do Nows: Small Tweaks That Make a Big Difference https://classteaching.wordpress.com/2025/10/17/do-nows-small-tweaks-that-make-a-big-difference/
q: At the start of every lesson, she would give her students approximately 10 questions to answer, based on prior learning. She taught me to same, so it is something I have been doing with my classes for a very long time.
While Do Now tasks do have a role in creating a calm and settled start to lessons they can, and should, be so much more than this.
It is important that not all of the questions relate to one lesson, as if a student missed that they will not be able to answer any of the questions.
If there are 15 questions and students routinely only have time to complete 5, we are telling them they don’t need to do all the work we set.
Also, consider not giving them the title until after the do now so that they focus solely on your questions, rather than attempting to be seen writing by studiously copying down the title.
I realised I often used to same questions when teaching a particular topic each year. This meant I was not tailoring it to the needs of my class that year.

t: A Daily Ritual of High Performers That You Likely Never Heard Of
q: But the best of the best add a unique wrinkle to this list of daily objectives.
In addition to articulating their goals for the day, they register the one question they want to answer during the day.
Research in performance psychology confirms that asking a meaningful daily question engages metacognition—the process of thinking about one’s thinking—which helps to clarify what truly matters most.
The ritual of starting the workday with a question to be answered transforms the day into a laboratory for growth and inquiry.
Avoid the generic and easy questions (like “What can I learn from today’s challenges?”) and go for the meaty questions that require you to hunt down a hard-to-find answer.

t: Teaching Is Absurd
q: We are constrained beings, limited in our time and energy and inability to multitask. Despite the ethos of our times, we can't do it all, be it all, complete it all, achieve it all. No amount of machinery or technology will ever change that either.

Each of them is a never-before-seen instance of humanity, fearfully and wonderfully wrought. They are mostly invisible creatures — we can see their faces and their work but not the immense web of experiences and relationships and chemicals and hormones and beliefs that make them them.
Teaching is absurd in that it entails us finite creatures working to connect dozens of boundlessly complex students with the cosmos-depths of disciplines in a rather dystopian context.

Because despite these absurdities, a massive good will come from our work this year, provided that we pursue it with the earnestness and craftsmanship and spirit our profession calls for. I'm not talking about doing it perfectly; I'm talking about doing it awake.

Good comes from regular classrooms led by regular teachers like you and me, even in the midst of the wildness of what we're doing. We really never know what good our work will do, but at the same time we can be confident that simple, good work in a classroom will do a kind of good that ripples on for generations.

t: Let Weighty Decisions Marinate While You Focus on Other Matters
q: Even when leaders are not actively trying to think through the decision or solve a problem, the brain continues processing it unconsciously in the background.
Research shows that the quality of decisions made after distraction, sleep, or inactivity is generally higher than those made by analysis without the benefit of downtime.

The first step to incorporate this marination process is to clearly identify the decision, problem, or opportunity you want the brain to work on. Articulating the problem statement in writing is essential.
If the decision is far out on the horizon, then occasionally repriming the brain by re-reading the statement can encourage the brain to keep the background analysis going.
Some of the world’s greatest thinkers, scientists, and artists describe these epiphanies in a host of books and manuscripts.

t: Is Your Class Valuable? Just Ask 'Em!
q: The great schools of today and tomorrow won't be differentiated by how they approach AI as much as they will be for the degree to which they help students Value the work of learning for many ways in which the work is good.

31 out of 34 teachers reported that their students gave similar responses across their classes. This wasn't the scattered feedback you'd expect from a qualitative survey. Students were seeing consistent value — or consistent problems — in each course.

When you see this kind of alignment in qualitative data, it tells you that you're reading something deeper than individual preferences. As we seek to align our teaching with the reality of our students' hearts, such insight is priceless.

It's not easy seeing multiple students report problems like these because, ultimately, these are ways we got in our students' way. But the bad news is good news when we look to how we might change our practice to get closer to "just right" amounts of challenge.
The feedback isn't about you as a person, it's about how your students are experiencing your class and about how you can better craft that experience in a way that cultivates the Value belief.

t: EAST — Four Simple Ways to Apply Behavioural Insights https://www.bi.team/publications/east-four-simple-ways-to-apply-behavioural-insights/
q: If you want to encourage a behaviour, make it easy, attractive, social and timely (EAST).
One study found that simply automating and streamlining parts of the university application process increased attendance rates from 28% to 36%.
For example, assuming parents are automatically signed up for a text message service detailing student progress resulted in a 95% enrollment rate, significantly higher than what leaders expected.

For teachers, the use of loss-framed incentives (giving a bonus upfront that must be returned if goals are not met) was more effective at improving student mathematics scores than standard end-of-year gain incentives, with positive effects lasting over five years.
Teachers must recognise that context remains crucial; interventions that are successful elsewhere may not work in a classroom.
The field faces a replication crisis, meaning results might fail to hold up to scrutiny.

t: Confident Leaders Must Learn to Hedge
q: Delivering honesty without emotional regulation is a recipe for intimidation and perceptions of insensitivity.
The answer to this dilemma is that they don’t have to be less direct or honest. They simply need to learn how to add a hedge.
Hedging shifts advocacy from an absolute claim to a subjective impression open to interpretation.
Hedges invite interpretation and dialogue rather than asserting an indisputable certainty.
Leaders who speak more indirectly and with lower confidence can harm their credibility by using hedges, and so can confident leaders who use too many of them, too often.

t: Using Diagnostic Classroom Assessment: One Question at a Time maths.com/resourcesnew/8.%20Research/Formative%20Assessment/Using%20Diagnostic%20Classr oom%20Assessment.pdf
q: Teachers must use questioning specifically designed to find out not just what students know, but what they do not know. Diagnostic items are powerful because an incorrect response provides specific insight into the nature of the student's misconceptions—inaccurate, incomplete, or partial understandings.

Formative assessment is defined as a process where evidence of learning is evoked and then used immediately to modify the teaching and learning activities. Teachers should use this evidence to adjust instruction as necessary, provide immediate feedback to individuals or the whole class, or structure the next lesson.

Teachers are encouraged to use individual diagnostic items efficiently and flexibly, using just “one item at a time” within the flow of day-to-day lessons. An item can be used at the start of a lesson to determine a baseline understanding, mid-way to decide between instructional paths, or near the end of instruction to identify struggling students.

When developing or selecting diagnostic items, the main concern is ensuring that incorrect answer choices (distractors) are related to common student misconceptions. Because the stakes are very low, teachers are freed from some constraints of high-stakes testing; for example, they can include two correct answers if it generates valuable classroom discussion.

Teachers must ensure they use valid items that specifically uncover misconceptions. Constructing these quality questions, where incorrect choices relate to common student errors, requires a “great deal of effort” and is critical for accurate diagnosis.

The main concern in developing diagnostic items is to ensure that the incorrect answer choices are connected to incorrect or incomplete understandings; and thus all student answers, not just the correct answers, provide insights into their learning

Key findings include a positive correlation between confidence and facility, with boys exhibiting higher confidence than girls and older students or socioeconomically disadvantaged students showing lower confidence, even when accounting for facility.

The study provides the first evidence of the hypercorrection effect—where highly confident errors are more likely to be corrected later—in an authentic school-mathematics context, with important implications for classroom learning practices.
Teachers should incorporate confidence assessment alongside diagnostic multiple-choice questions. This feature can serve as an innovative formative assessment tool.
Finally, we found the first evidence for the hypercorrection effect in an authentic mathematics learning context.

q: Conditions of learning that make performance improve rapidly often fail to support long-term retention and transfer, whereas conditions that create challenges and slow the rate of apparent learning often optimize long-term retention and transfer
Optimising learning often requires deviating from standard practices and introducing conditions that challenge learners.
Tests should be viewed as a vehicle of learning and not solely a vehicle of assessment.
It is critical to ensure the learner has the necessary background knowledge or skills to respond to the difficulty successfully; otherwise, the challenge becomes an undesirable difficulty.

Instruction should aim to maximise the gain of storage strength (how entrenched a memory is) rather than just rapidly boosting retrieval strength (current accessibility, which dictates immediate performance).
Interleaving, even though it may slow initial performance, leads to superior long-term retention and transfer, potentially by forcing learners to notice similarities and differences among concepts.

t: Integrating New Team Members Into the Social Fabric of the Organization
q: Becoming immersed in the fabric of an organization is largely about relationships.
The faster new team members develop strong ties to top performers, the more likely they are to commit, succeed, and stay.
But the best organizations are much more intentional about launching a new team member relationally.
This role goes by many names in organizations, including sponsor, immersion guide, onboarding buddy, peer mentor, onboarding captain, senior guide, and relationship coach.
Tapping into the social network of the organization is perhaps the best predictor of a new team member’s long-term success.

t: Cognitive Load Theory: The Story of a Research Programme https://www.researchgate.net/publication/294106592_Story_of_a_Research_Program
q: The worked example effect demonstrated clearly that showing learners how to do something was far better than having them work it out themselves.

The research suggests that conventional problem solving, particularly using a means-ends analysis strategy, heavily overloads the limited capacity of working memory, preventing the transfer of knowledge to long-term memory (learning).
Teachers should leverage the Worked Examples Effect, where learners who study worked examples perform better on test problems than those who solve the same problems themselves.

For advanced learners (experts), worked examples can become redundant; teachers should introduce problem solving practice or completion problems (partially completed problems) as learners gain expertise (Expertise Reversal Effect).
Teachers should explicitly show students how to solve problems rather than expecting them to discover the knowledge themselves through minimal guidance.

t: When Should You Prop Up a Weak Team Member
q: The decision to prop up and support a weak team member is a dilemma all leaders wrestle with at some point.
First, it is important that the underperformance stems from a skill gap or unclear expectations rather than a poor attitude.
Second, the team member must show they are coachable, open to feedback, and have a strong desire to improve.
If the effort results in dependency or decreased accountability, investing in this team member will erode trust and create jealousy within the team.
Leaders who make this call without input from the team members who must carry the weight stand a good chance of creating bitterness and resentment.

t: Abruptly Ending a Hostile Conversation
q: Once the other party has crossed the line or continues along an unpleasant path, it is time to end the conversation.
One expression lends itself to this situation and provides a fast escape while maintaining a positive ending: “Have a great day!
The expression “Have a great day!” clearly signals that the conversation or exchange has come to an end. It doesn’t provoke a response, nor does it invite a reaction.
The calm control of an abrupt ending with a statement like “Have a great day!” neutralizes the negativity and prevents more inflammatory comments from being traded.
Good leaders pre-decide that once a hostile party crosses a boundary in a conversation, the best course of action is to withdraw.

t: A Novel Way to Express Gratitude
q: Finding a novel expression of gratitude that truly lands with others is not always obvious.

The next time you want to express your gratitude for a team member, consider giving them a comprehensive list of their strengths, as you see them, simply but powerfully articulated on a sheet of paper.
When I think of you and the many contributions, talents, and skills you bring to our team, these are your strengths that stand out to me.
Learning how a leader views their strengths can be an amazing experience for a team member and expresses the leader’s gratitude like very few other expressions can.
Don’t be surprised if the team member not only saves the note but pulls it out to read it whenever they need a boost of confidence or validation about their value.

t: How To Handle A Student Who Doesn't Do Their Work
q: Anything and everything you do directly—as in approaching and engaging with the student—is bound to fail. Because it doesn’t come from within the student.
Motivation and desire to do the work must come from them. It must be their choice and of their volition.
Instead, let them just sit there. That’s right. Once you send your students off to do their independent work, you’re finished speaking or offering additional help.
You will not inflate any grade. You will mark the exact score they earned on their report card, essay, math assignment, reading assessment, etc.
Do this every day. Get really good at it. And you’ll never again have students sitting and doing nothing.

t: Are We Facing the Worst Generation of Parents?
q: Though thankfully they remain a significant minority, the impact of those parents is profound. Theirs is a world in which their children can do no wrong and where their children’s disruptive conduct is defended at every turn.
In a post entitled Blamelessness, written in 2008, I described a philosophy based on the idea that children are natural saints.

It was necessary to come up with imaginative explanations of why children are not responsible for their behaviour, thereby allowing them to be innocent victims even when they are observed to be behaving like complete bastards.
This philosophy declined in influence (at least in secondary schools) once Ofsted and Local Authorities were no longer enforcing it.
The latest version of it is the one in which badly behaved children are described as needing opportunities to 'regulate' rather than sanctions.
Many of today's teenagers have parents who attended school in the 2000s. This is the era described in the early posts on my blog.

t: Are You Rewarding Performance Theater Over Real Performance
q: Some of the best performers keep their heads down and refuse to promote themselves. They believe the quality of their work is the best advertisement for their value.
Rewarding real performance over performance theatrics is critically important for retaining top talent and creating a workplace that focuses on meritocracy and not splash.
When given the opportunity to speak, they focus more on the story than on the tangible impact of their work.
Top performers are trusted by peers to handle critical tasks and responsibilities and are regularly called upon to fill in or stand by in case they are needed.

t: Good Leaders Develop an Editorial Mindset
q: To uphold their commitment to quality, good leaders operate as editors. It may be the most important slice of what they do as leaders.
As editors, leaders shape and refine the messages, ideas, and viewpoints of others to make them stronger and more impactful.
Not surprisingly, editorially skilled leaders run better meetings. They curate the most important topics and content and cut away any unnecessary issues or discussion points
You don’t have to be a great writer to be a great editor. That’s because they involve different skill sets.
If the essence of great work is continual revising and improvement, exceptional leaders do the editing.

t: Can a Team Be Too Stable
q: But the opposite problem can present its own unique set of problems. Some teams and organizations actually create too much stability.
A team or organization that is too heavily populated by senior and highly tenured colleagues often creates a leadership nightmare.
Not surprisingly, top-heavy teams normally have little room for advancement, so opportunities for promotion or new roles become limited.
The best path is not to allow a team to become too top-heavy in the first place.
Great teams are made up of a mix of early-career and later-career team members.

t: Team Members Who Sugar-Coat Their Feedback to Colleagues
q: Team members who prioritize being liked, projecting positivity, and showing support for their colleagues will often sugar-coat their feedback and refrain from truthful criticism.
So, when asked for feedback, they pull their punches and highlight only the positives as a way to maintain social harmony and to avoid damaging their relationships.
The best leaders know a secret. Under the right questioning, even feedback-evasive team members will offer more candid views to their colleagues.
These questions are difficult to duck or dismiss, although the most reluctant peers will still find a way to avoid them, usually by claiming they can’t think of an answer.
Good leaders don’t accept this Texas two-step. They push for a more constructive answer anyway.

t: Research Bite #41: Secondary School Mathematics Teachers' Accuracy at Predicting Student Errors
q: The paper investigates how well mathematics teachers can anticipate the frequency of student mistakes on diagnostic multiple-choice questions.

Researchers found that while teachers were generally skilled at identifying the underlying errors and misconceptions the questions were designed to elicit, their prediction accuracy significantly improved over time with repeated practice.

Professional development focused on developing the ability to anticipate student errors (such as predicting responses to diagnostic questions) can lead to rapid and significant improvement in predictive accuracy.
This type of professional development is easy to conduct, requires little preparation, and a teacher could carry it out independently without needing external funding.
Teachers should exercise caution because the study had a small sample size (seven participants), limiting generalisation.

We conclude that professional development focused on developing teachers' ability to anticipate student errors could lead to rapid improvement in teachers' error prediction and be potentially valuable in improving their classroom teaching.

t: The Uncommon Initiative of High Talent
q: Speak to experienced leaders and ask them to describe the most talented team members they have ever worked with, and they will tell you that those colleagues took uncommon initiative.
The most talented team members ignore traditional hierarchy and, without thought for approval or acceptance, work to identify the needs, gaps, and opportunities that are not obvious to others.
Uncommon initiative typically shares four critical ingredients: one part curiosity and openness, one part courage and boldness, one part proactive purpose, and one part creative ideation.
The highest talent doesn’t think that way or care about acceptance or deployment. When they see a big gap or opportunity, they seize the initiative.
They know that real opportunity never knocks. They open the door anyway.

t: Why Humor Is A Powerful Classroom Management Strategy ement-strategy/
q: Creating a classroom your students love being part of combined with an unwavering commitment to accountability.
When you tell a joke or recount a funny story, powerful, behavior-influencing rapport begins to grow immediately.
Today’s students are anxious. Smart phones, social media use, various traumas and familial pressures. Humor attacks stress at its root, melting it away from the inside.
The answer is that in the absence of accountability—and how to effectively implement it—you’ve already lost control.
It doesn’t make sense to add fuel to the fire with jokes and funny stories until and unless you apply the only classroom management approach that works wherever and whoever you teach.

t: Celebrating Colleagues for Personal Milestones Can Establish a Dangerous Precedent
q: Once the organization, team, or leadership endorses, sponsors, or funds such an event, it becomes symbolic that they do so in the future for everyone with the same good or bad news.
Those who perceive that they’ve been treated differently will often keep it to themselves. But the taste of dissatisfaction often stays with them.
Good leaders don’t wash their hands of this dilemma by avoiding all recognition and celebration. Instead, they encourage others to arrange such celebrations on their own
The leaders, too, can partake in the event as long as they represent themselves and not the organization or team.
The best leaders believe everyone counts and prove it by the precedents they set or don’t.

t: Team Members Who Consistently Misinterpret Your Directions
q: It may be that some team members are simply resistant to directions. Others may deliberately thumb their nose at the leader and chart their own path.
People who consistently misinterpret directions, instructions, and other messages simply hear what they want to hear.
Instead of explaining what they want to see in the future, they get more specific. They ask for specific actions.
This request, like so many other directions that get ignored or misinterpreted, suggests inaction or what the other party should NOT do.
Asking people to act is a much harder message to misinterpret than a request not to act.

t: Definitions Contain Limited Information
q: It is not unusual for tests to ask students to define a term or concept. However, these type of questions tend to generate informationally poor responses.
We do not know whether the student just learnt the definition by rote, with no real understanding of the concept.
A definition does not reveal anything about whether they understand the boundaries of a concept or what would count as a non-example.
It doesn't take an English teacher to know that metaphors and similes are often confused. The student's answer tells us nothing about whether this common 'non-example' is understood.
Asking students to compare things helps tease out whether they understand the core tenets of a concept and where the boundaries are.
None of the above questions are perfect, but then there is no such thing as a perfect assessment question.

t: Beyond Getting Their Attention
q: Students can only learn what they are paying attention to. This prompt gives them a social cue that what the teacher is going to be talking about is important - and so requires their attention.
Rather than drawing attention to this and calling it out in front of the whole class e.g. 'Nick.focus on me now!', take the least invasive intervention.

If students know that your explanation is going to consist of them having to listen to you for five minutes, without any input from them, the reality is, there's no requirement for them to pay attention.

Cognitive scientist Daniel Willingham describes stories as being 'psychologically privileged'. This means our brains are wired to process stories differently and more effectively than other forms of information.
Once you have set students to work on a task, move to a position in the room where all students will be in your field of view.
When it comes to effective teaching, there is very little more important than securing and maintaining attention.

t: 3-Read Friday #86: Securing Attention, Definitions, and the Post-Literate Society
q: Many schools I visit use things like narrated countdowns to focus students’ attention. This is all well and good, but how do we then maintain that attention?
I have considered definitions a tad overrated for a while now. Sure, students can parrot back the definition of a polygon or a quadratic equation, but do they understand what it actually means?
I wouldn’t describe this as the most optimistic of posts, but it is certainly a powerful one.
James cites evidence about the decline in reading in general, the changing nature of the books we do read, and the implications for humanity. Spoiler alert: they are not good.
In this post, Matthew shares some tests of conceptual understanding that go beyond recall of a definition.

t: How I Start 99% of My Classes
q: I don't know of a better class starter/do-now/bell-ringer/warm-up than provisional writing. In my classes, this looks like me providing prompts (typically three) and students getting a set number of minutes to write toward the prompts.

As a writer who has published over a million words myself, I know that quantity precedes quality. And also, for many of my students who don't believe they are writers or that they can write, piling up words over the first weeks of school is an effective fertilizer for writing-conducive beliefs (e.g., Belonging, Efficacy) to start growing.

Writing 100 words in five minutes is one of those special kinds of things you can ask students to do that A) is perceived as difficult by many students and, at the same time, B) is actually not difficult (20 words per minute is all that's required; most people can write at this rate even with their non-dominant hand).
I like the PR angle because it signals that in this class, we'll compete against our past selves, not against one another.
Like virtually all of my approaches to teaching, what I've shared here isn't novel or ground-breaking. But it works very well.

t: Leaders Who Discount Long-Term Rewards and Risks
q: Temporal discounting is the process by which a person values immediate rewards more highly than rewards that are delayed or given in the future, even when those rewards are larger or more beneficial.
This tendency explains why people sometimes make impulsive decisions, choosing short-term gratification over long-term gain.
Leaders who succumb to the effects of discounting prioritize short-term outcomes while often sacrificing future objectives and gains.
They also commit resources to longer-term initiatives, such as talent development, innovation, and process improvement, to offset any attempt at discounting.
Temporal discounting is yet another enemy of great leadership and decision-making.

t: Pointing the Hubble Telescope at Our Classrooms
q: So if students are, in fact, these once-in-infinity combinations of mind and emotion and relationships and body and will, and you multiply that by every person in the class, and then take that and multiply it by every experience any of these people have ever had, you start to get an idea of your classroom's motivational context.

Galaxies have about one hundred billion stars in them apiece. One hundred billion of our suns, multiplied by thousands, multiplied by all the rest of the night sky beyond the pinhead-sized spot Hubble looked at. Some scientists — scientists — even go so far as to say that the number of stars in the universe may be infinite. Stupefyingly grandiose is a fair summary of our cosmological context.

And that's what the classroom context is like. The more you learn about teaching and people and your discipline and yourself, the more you think, Oooookay. There is a lot happening here. And all of this context is influencing student motivation all of the time.

The Five Key Beliefs give us a methodology for finding signals within that noise; we have a lens filter that helps us to see the layer of motivation and intervene intelligently. The Five Key Beliefs help us turn chaos into concept and therein find agency when faced with the difficulty of student demotivation.

Think of Five Key Beliefs work as the sending of signals. Amidst the complexity of a classroom, we want to be consistently producing signals — through our words and our actions, our lessons and our assignments, and our policies and procedures — that we're credible, the work is valuable, each student belongs here, and smart Effort can yield growth and success and the success of growth (Efficacy).
Folks who work at radio towers don't control whether or not their signal is received, but they have complete control over whether or not the signal is sent. This must be the teacher's mindset.

t: Can People Be Too Positive
q: When this upbeat attitude becomes excessive, psychologists call it Toxic Positivity. Research suggests it carries a host of negative influences.
Expressions such as “look on the bright side,” “just stay positive,” “it could be worse,
cheer up,” and “everything happens for a reason” may come from good intentions, but they dismiss the negative feelings felt by others.
Such toxic positivity can also erode authentic relationships by discouraging open communication and emotional honesty
When leaders have this mindset, team members often feel pressured to appear upbeat and cheerful, even in difficult or painful circumstances
Optimism is never an excuse for ignoring a serious problem or obstacle.

t: Research Bite #40: Those Who Understand: Knowledge Growth in Teaching
q: Shulman begins by confronting the historical slight against teachers, arguing that the profession has been plagued by the notion that those who cannot perform simply teach, contrasting this view with an earlier Aristotelian perspective where teaching was considered the ultimate demonstration of knowledge.
The ultimate test of understanding rests on the ability to transform one's knowledge into teaching.

Teachers need an "armamentarium" of powerful representations, including analogies, illustrations, examples, explanations, and demonstrations, specifically tailored to make topics comprehensible to students.
Cases act as prototypes (exemplifying principles), precedents (capturing wisdom of practice), and parables (conveying norms and values).
Principles (propositions) are often decontextualized and may collide in practice (e.g., wait-time vs. pace), limiting their utility.

t: Are You an Objective Decision-Maker
q: In comparison to other decision-makers, leaders viewed as objective are more trusted to reach the best possible decision.
Scholars contend that no one can be completely objective, as their beliefs and experience can’t be entirely ignored or disregarded.
They emphasize that the information used to reach a decision be provable, testable, or verifiable.
This focus on objectivity influences leaders to work hard at suppressing misleading intuition that springs from their experience.
Objectivity inspires confidence in both the decision and the decision-maker.

t: The Reciprocity of Liking and Team Cohesion
q: As it turns out, the most likable people have the longest lists of people they like. By expressing liking first, people respond in kind.
Research behind the Reciprocity of Liking proves that people are attracted to and like others who express liking for them.
This reciprocity effect occurs in digital interaction as well. People have a strong tendency to reciprocate “likes” on a social media platform, even with people they don’t know.
Colleagues perceive genuine compliments, positive feedback, attentive listening, making time for small talk, inclusive language (we, our), a willingness to offer assistance
Leaders who encourage more of the behaviors of liking and display them in their own interactions create the most positive workplaces and most cohesive teams.

t: School Improvement Starts Here: Behaviour, Attention, Participation, and Memory 2025
q: Behaviour comes first because, well, it has to come first. Nothing is possible in a school where behaviour is poor.
Poor behaviour is a lead weight on school improvement, and there is little point focusing on anything else until it is fixed.
This strategy, simply called Name at End questioning, communicates that all students have to be listening to the question, as they do not know who it will go to.
The most powerful of these strategies is the use of mini-whiteboards, and leaders should quickly move towards a target of mini-whiteboards being used in almost every lesson.
However good your lessons are, without a long term memory strategy, they are worth very little. Humans forget things, and they forget things fast.
The issues of behaviour, attention, participation and memory are shared by all schools and transcend the idiosyncrasies that make schools such varied and fascinating places to visit and work in.

t: Is a Noisy Classroom a Thinking Classroom?
q: When I first started teaching English 20 years ago, a fairly uncontested idea was the notion that “a noisy classroom is a thinking classroom”.
A new study in Cognition (Marko et al., 2026) shows just how costly that particular noise can be if students are trying to think hard about something.

The researchers found that when we are trying to retrieve certain concepts from memory to generate new ideas, the greatest interference comes not from meaningless sounds (traffic, humming, background tones etc), but surprisingly from meaningful speech.
This creates interference not by stealing attention, but by creating competing neural activity in the same systems you need for thinking.
Students discussing related topics create maximum interference for peers working on similar material - exactly the opposite of what we’d assume about “productive classroom talk.
Rather, it’s a call for cognitive hospitality; creating learning environments that honour both the social and solitary dimensions of thinking.

t: How To Get Every Student To Participate
q: 19th Century psychologist and Harvard professor William James believed so strongly that teaching was a mutual process that when his students’ participation waned he would lie down in class as if to take a nap.
So how do you get everyone involved? Luckily, there is a surefire method. It’s also easy and has the added benefit of keeping them wide awake.
I recommend a quick shuffle after every question. This way, a student could potentially be called on again, thereby keeping them perpetually on their toes.
Great teachers don’t let students hide. Participation isn’t a choice. No excuses.
In this classroom, you will be called on so you better be ready for it.

t: Getting Better at Tough Conversations
q: Holding people accountable, delivering news of unwanted change, and sharing decisions that disappoint are some of the many topics considered “tough” for leaders to navigate.

The best leaders reframe the entire conversation to change this script. Instead of viewing the conversation as confronting a difficult topic or issue, they think of it as a collaborative problem-solving exchange.
They place themselves inside the problem, issue, or news by using the pronouns “We” and “I” instead of “You.
Viewing a tough conversation as a problem to be collaboratively resolved together is automatically less judgmental and critical
Good leaders solve a problem together with the other party when they deliver a tough message.

t: Leaders Who Veto Decisions
q: Good leaders reserve their veto power for situations and decisions that would irreparably harm the organization or undermine a major initiative.
A veto says loudly that the leader believes they are smarter, wiser, and more clairvoyant than the team entrusted with the decision.

Unless the group becomes convinced of the leader’s wisdom for standing in the way, a veto will erode trust, diminish future participation, and leave the impression that the team’s input is undervalued.
The best leaders even go one step further. They ask the team to withdraw their decision based on their argument.
A leader who asserts their decision rights for any other reason is taking a big gamble.
